name: Olive
lede: Olive is a dull, brownish green named for the olive tree and its fruit; on screens it is a bright yellow-green, while the charts of the past kept it far browner and greyer.

sections.title: A fruit's name
sections.body:
*Olive* names the tree and its fruit, and the color word follows the fruit [4][15]. Mineralogy kept the link: olivine, the most abundant material in the earth's mantle, is named for the color of pale green olives [4]. The gem [[gem:peridot|peridot]] is gem-quality olivine, and about ninety per cent of known peridots come from one Native American reservation in the United States [4].

Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates the English color word to 1613 [10]. The word was always loose at the edges: Paterson's entry for *bracken* describes an olive-brown, and his entry for *chloroxanthous* gives a green or olive and yellow [15].

sections.title: Grass green with brown
sections.body:
The most exact old definition is Werner's, as Patrick Syme presented it in his *Nomenclature of Colours* [1]. Number 59 of the greens, olive green, is grass green mixed with much brown [1]. Syme's examples are the foliage of lignum vitae and two minerals, epidote and olivine ore [1].

The same system has an olive brown, number 109, which Syme also called clove brown and used for the head and neck of a male kestrel [2]. His hair brown is olive brown mixed with ash grey [2]. Other lists of the period kept olive green: Cleaveland's 1816 list of 80 colors places it between asparagus green and oil green [3].

So the color was a family of dulled, browned greens before it was a single swatch [1][2]. The nearest related names in our library are [[olive-green]], [[olive-brown]] and [[olive-grey]] [10].

sections.title: Drab and olive drab
sections.body:
*Drab* was once the technical term for a hue on the middle line between olive and puce, and only later came to mean dullness itself [5]. St Clair's glossary defines olive drab as green with plenty of grey and brown [9]. That is close to Werner's brown-green, and it is the olive that dyers and tailors meant, more than the yellower swatch on a screen [1][9].

A 1529 inventory of Hernán Cortés's goods lists a coverlet of scarlet and olive-colored cloth, which shows the word in use for cloth early in the sixteenth century [13]. The colormaker and theorist George Field counted olive among his tertiary pigments, alongside citrine and russet [14].

sections.title: In paint and pigment
sections.body:
Olive turns up in painting mostly as a mixed or accidental color. Ball describes chrome green as a cheap mixture of Prussian blue and chrome yellow, with results from a harsh green down to olive [6]. The Pigment Compendium calls chromium oxide an opaque, dull olive green [8].

Burnt verdigris is described by the chemist Salter in 1869 as an olive-coloured oxide of copper, and the calcined form of Schweinfurt green is also olive [8]. Gauguin, in Tahiti, found burnt ochre indispensable for painting the olive skin of the people he met [7]. Where to look: olive is what a green becomes when brown is mixed into it, by hand or by age [1][8].

sections.title: The tree of peace
sections.body: In medieval symbolism the olive was a tree of peace, one of many trees given a meaning in orchard imagery [11]. The flag of the United Nations shows the world between two olive branches, and Pastoureau reads this as part of blue's calm, peaceful symbolism [11]. These meanings belong to the tree and the branch rather than to the color olive, which carries none of them in the books we checked [11].

sections.title: Which olive is the swatch?
sections.body:
The swatch here is CSS `olive`, #808000, which is bright and yellow: lightness 52, chroma 58 [10]. The old charts disagree with it, and with each other [10]. Ridgway's 1912 olive is a dark, greyish #645F46, lightness 40 and chroma 15, and his olive green is a more yellow-brown #6D6D3F [10]. Werner's aged swatch for olive green reads as a cool #67765B, while the Wikipedia olive green is a light #B5B35C, lightness 71 [10].

Five sources give five olives, and the CSS one is the second brightest, after Wikipedia's [10]. When a painter or a tailor says olive, the Ridgway and Werner end of that range is the safer guess [1][10].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, 18 contain this exact olive: a color within six units of #808000 (ΔE 2000) covering at least five per cent of the canvas [12]. None of the 3,619 works made before 1600 do [12]. The earliest match is Frans Snijders's *Larder with Game, Fruit, Vegetables and a Servant* from 1616, where it covers 9 per cent [[painting:smk-KMSsp208|the larder]] [12].

The surprise is geography. Five of the 18 are Indian paintings, although India is about 3 per cent of the archive (721 works), and one is Tibetan [12]. The largest field is in a Tibetan-style *God Shiva in His Ferocious Aspect as Mahakala Dancing* from about 1700, where olive covers 47 per cent of the canvas [[painting:cma-132820|Mahakala]] [12]. In European painting the match is rare: Canaletto's *English Landscape Capriccio with a Palace* of 1754 holds it on 22 per cent [[painter:canaletto|Canaletto]] [12].

These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a color match and not a pigment test [12].
